tip: English fills the bottle – Hindi flips it: बोतल में ठंडा पानी भरा है (botal mein thanda paani bhara hai = in the bottle cold water is filled). The container gets में (mein), the water is the subject.
Hindi position words come after their word, not before: यहाँ से (yahaan se = here from) = from here. Every from, on, in trails its word – mez par, subah se.
For breakfast is नाश्ते में (naashte mein = in breakfast), not ke liye. Meals take में (mein): you make things in breakfast, in lunch.
No word for to with going: हवाई अड्डा कैसे जाएँ (hawai adda kaise jaaen = how to go airport). Destinations of jaana usually take nothing – ghar jao, school jao.
Hindi says where things are placed, not that they exist: फ्रिज में दूध रखा है (fridge mein doodh rakha hai = milk is kept in the fridge) is the everyday way to say there is milk.
तक (tak) means both until and by: शाम तक (shaam tak) here is by evening – a deadline. Shaam tak kaam kiya would be until evening. Context picks the reading.
Trains walk in Hindi: चलती है (chalti hai = moves) is how the train departs from the platform. चलना (chalna) covers vehicles and machines – a working watch chalti hai too.
English lumps all uncles together – Hindi is precise: फूफाजी (phoophaji) is specifically your father's sister's husband. The जी (ji) on the end adds respect.
Doubling stretches a word: दूर-दूर तक (door-door tak = up to far-far) = far and wide. Hindi repeats words for spread – kabhi-kabhi is sometimes, dheere-dheere is slowly.
Hindi meets from people: रूपा से मिलिए (Roopa se miliye = meet Roopa). मिलना (milna) always takes से (se), never a plain object like English meet.
से (se) doubles as by for any means: बस से (bus se) = by bus. Card se, haath se (by hand) – transport, payment, and tools all take से.
की (ki) agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: सुषमा की किताब (Sushma ki kitaab) uses feminine की because kitaab is feminine – Sushma's own gender is irrelevant.
Hindi has no verb for to have – people just exist in your space: मेरे ऑफिस में बहुत अच्छे साथी हैं (mere office mein bahut achche saathi hain = in my office are very good colleagues).
से (se) also marks causes: दर्द होने से (dard hone se = from pain happening) = because of the pain. Verb + hone se is the everyday due to.
Phones close in Hindi: फ़ोन बंद हो गया (phone band ho gaya = the phone became closed) = it died or switched off. बंद (band) covers closed and off – shops, lights, phones.
पर (par) means on, but it is also Hindi's at: बस स्टॉप पर (bus stop par) = at the bus stop. There is no separate word – station par, ghar par.
Times of day take को (ko), not में: शाम को (shaam ko = to evening) means in the evening. Subah ko, raat ko – no equivalent of the English in appears.
Next to is a body word: सुरेश के बगल में (Suresh ke bagal mein = in Suresh's side) – bagal is your side or flank. Many Hindi place phrases sit inside a noun like this.
Hindi builds before as from + earlier: दशहरे से पहले (Dashahre se pahle = from Dussehra earlier) = before Dussehra. After works the same way – ke baad.
पर (par) usually means on or at, but after a verb form it means upon: छींक आने पर (chheenk aane par = on a sneeze coming) = when you sneeze.
Seeing the doctor is showing: डॉक्टर को दिखाना है (doctor ko dikhaana hai = have to show to the doctor). You show yourself to doctors in Hindi – dikhaana, not dekhna.
